summary:
El Salvador has no Gender Identity Law and no legal recognition of gender identity. A trans visitor carrying documents issued in another country has no domestic mechanism through which those documents could be aligned or challenged. In 2022 the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court ordered the Name Law reformed so that individuals could change their names to match their gender identity, holding the existing regime unconstitutional because it discriminated on the basis of gender, after a case brought by a transgender activist in 2016. As of 2023 the Legislative Assembly had enacted nothing, so transgender Salvadorans still cannot update official papers.

The penal code carries an enhanced penalty for bias-motivated killing. In September 2015 the National Assembly approved reforms under which homicides motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender draw 30 to 60 years under Article 129. A 2015 hate crime law added sexual orientation and gender identity provisions to the Criminal Code, carrying three to six years' imprisonment. A 2018 Institutional Policy for the Care of the LGBT Population allows LGBT people to file legal complaints against discrimination.

Human Rights Watch reported in 2020 and 2021 that El Salvador, with Guatemala and Honduras, fails to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, driving asylum claims to the United States; the reports document obstacles to obtaining protection. Police have shown blatant refusal to cooperate in LGBT death investigations. About 500 hate crimes against LGBT people were reported between 1998 and 2015, with many unreported. Gang violence includes targeting of LGBT people through physical and sexual assault, forced recruitment, and extortion for safety.

The death of Camila Díaz Córdova, a transgender Salvadoran woman, was prosecuted as a hate crime; activists called it an advance toward El Salvador's first hate-crime homicide conviction. On 28 July 2020 a San Salvador judge found three police officers guilty of the January 2019 killing and sentenced each to 20 years, the first homicide conviction in El Salvador for killing a transgender person.

Since the state of exception began in March 2022, trans women arbitrarily captured in mass raids have been held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. Jennifer, arrested on 14 April 2022 in San Salvador, was held first at the El Penalito police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out with another trans woman, Rosa, for outdoor punishment drills while handcuffed and forced to squat in the sun, and denied her access to an HIV clinic; a judge freed her after about four months, finding the arrest unsupported, while Rosa remains imprisoned. Socorro Jurídico Humanista and Cristosal link the abuse to the absence of a Gender Identity Law.

Prison conditions are explicitly hostile: homosexual inmates are strictly forbidden from dressing or behaving in an effeminate manner, and men are targeted by police officers, soldiers and prison guards for effeminate behaviour or dress through unwarranted searches, theft of property, sexual assault and other physical violence. In the 1999 investigation of Doris and Maricela, the two transvestites were forced to wear men's clothing for their hearing.

Hospital specialists frequently dismiss trans patients' problems as a side effect of being transgender, and patients are sometimes made to wait longer or denied care. Transgender health care access is severely restricted: there is a lack of protocols and programmes for hormone therapy and sex reassignment surgery, and one study found that many trans women did not seek medical help after suffering side effects from surgeries, having learned not to trust the system. In April 2009 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance published guidelines banning discrimination against LGBT and HIV-positive people in health services, and a 2009 national HIV/AIDS health plan included a prohibition on sexual orientation-based discrimination in health care.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised: the Family Code's Article 11 defines marriage as a heterosexual union, individuals may adopt but same-sex couples cannot adopt as a couple, and the Law on Family Violence does not apply to same-sex couples. Since 2006 there have been proposals to amend the Constitution to restrict recognition even of same-sex couples married legally abroad. Two legal challenges to the ban were dismissed on technical and procedural grounds on 20 December 2016 and 17 January 2019, although the Constitutional Court declared a proposed marriage ban unlawful in January 2018 and admitted a lawsuit for recognition of same-sex marriage for a hearing in August 2019, following a January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion holding same-sex marriage to be a human right.

A 2013 study showed that 62 per cent of Salvadorans do not accept homosexuality and 85 per cent believe it acceptable to attack a transgender individual on the basis of their identity. A 2010 poll showed 10 per cent support for legalising same-sex marriage, and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 19 per cent support.
tangentialFactors: Human Rights Watch places El Salvador alongside Guatemala and Honduras as states that fail to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, and links that failure to asylum claims filed in the United States. The January 2018 advisory opinion of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, holding same-sex marriage to be a human right, is the regional legal backdrop against which Salvadoran courts have considered recognition claims. The peer-reviewed longitudinal dataset 'Denied deaths' (Arévalo et al., 2024) profiles crimes, victims and perpetrators of homicides against LGBTI+ people in El Salvador across 2000-2020 and is the principal academic record for the period.
localsOnly:
Transgender Salvadorans cannot update official papers: the 2022 Supreme Court order to reform the Name Law had produced no legislative action as of 2023. Sexuality is absent from the school curriculum, LGBT students drop out at high rates, and some have been expelled for their sexuality and identity; no known universities or graduate programmes offer Sexuality Studies. Where LGBT children come out, families may subject them to conversion therapy or family prayers, and when these fail families sometimes expel the child and sever all connections. LGBT community members report suicide ideation and attempts at higher rates than the general population, and psychological care is often experienced as insecure and prejudiced, frequently arriving as conversion therapy.

A national HIV/AIDS policy has developed since 2005, with the first National HIV testing day established in 2007; gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood, though policy prohibits those who 'engage in risky behaviours' from donating. Entre Amigos organised El Salvador's first Gay Pride Parade in June 1997 to commemorate the massacre of trans women in the 1980s, and San Salvador authorised permanent rainbow paintings at several crossroads in July 2017.
outOfScopeNotes: The 2022 Supreme Court order on the Name Law is unresolved: the Legislative Assembly had taken no action as of 2023, and no later enactment is sourced here. The lawsuit for recognition of same-sex marriage admitted for a hearing in August 2019 has no sourced outcome. The proposals since 2006 to amend the Constitution to restrict recognition of same-sex couples married abroad are not sourced as enacted. The 'Denied deaths' dataset's homicide figures for 2000-2020 are not itemised in this record. Whether the 2015 hate-crime penalty framework has produced convictions beyond the Camila Díaz Córdova case is not sourced.
